subject: surgery
title: Metastatic Cervical Nodes, Unknown Primary, and Ludwig Angina

steps.tx: In adult patients presenting with an asymptomatic, firm, non-tender neck mass, the overriding clinical premise is Skandalakis' famous rule of eighties. Under this statistical maxim, eighty percent of non-thyroid lateral neck swellings in adults are neoplastic, eighty percent of these neoplasms are malignant, and eighty percent of these malignancies represent **metastatic cervical lymphadenopathy** from primary squamous cell carcinomas of the upper aerodigestive tract, demanding rigorous systematic mucosal search.
steps.say: Under the rule of eighties, eighty percent of adult lateral neck masses are neoplastic, and eighty percent of those are metastatic carcinomas from head and neck mucosal primaries.

nodes.label: Adult Non-Thyroid Lateral Neck Mass
80% Are Neoplastic Lesions
80% of Neoplasms Are Malignant
80% of Malignancies Are Metastatic Nodes
Primary Focus in Upper Aerodigestive Mucosa

steps.tx: The anatomical level of a metastatic cervical lymph node reliably predicts the location of the primary occult carcinoma. Level one nodes drain the lips, anterior oral cavity, and skin of the face. Level two upper deep jugular nodes receive lymph from the oropharynx, hypopharynx, larynx, and supraglottis. Conversely, isolated **Virchow node metastasis** in the left supraclavicular fossa (Troisier sign) signals advanced infraclavicular intra-abdominal or pelvic malignancy, classically gastric adenocarcinoma, transmitted via the thoracic duct.
steps.say: The level of a neck node points directly to the primary cancer. Level two nodes drain the oropharynx and larynx, while left supraclavicular nodes herald intra-abdominal cancer.

rows: Level I (Submandibular)
Oral tongue, floor of mouth, lower lip, buccal mucosa
Chewing tobacco exposure; low risk from infraclavicular organs
Level II (Upper Jugular)
Tonsil, base of tongue, supraglottic larynx, pyriform fossa
HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer frequently forms cystic level II nodes
Level III & IV (Mid & Low)
Hypopharynx, subglottis, thyroid gland, cervical esophagus
Aggressive trans-glottic cancers; routine central compartment spread
Level IV Left (Virchow)
Stomach, pancreas, ovary, testicle, lung, colon
Troisier sign: hematogenous and thoracic duct dissemination of GI tumors
Level V (Posterior)
Nasopharynx, posterior scalp skin, thyroid carcinoma
Epstein-Barr virus-driven nasopharyngeal carcinoma (Fossa of Rosenmuller)

steps.tx: When a patient presents with biopsy-proven metastatic cervical lymphadenopathy without an obvious tumor on clinical examination, the condition is classified as carcinoma of unknown primary. The primary diagnostic investigation of choice is **fine-needle aspiration cytology**. An absolute oncological rule strictly proscribes open incisional or excisional node biopsy prior to panendoscopy, because open biopsy tears fascial barriers, causes tumor seeding into soft tissues, and worsens overall regional control.
steps.say: Fine-needle aspiration cytology is the mandatory first step for an unknown primary. Open node biopsy is strictly forbidden because it breaches fascial planes and compromises cure.

left.title: Fine-Needle Aspiration Cytology
points: Performs needle aspiration without incising deep cervical fascia
Preserves tissue architecture and boundaries of neck levels
Identifies carcinoma, melanoma, lymphoma, and HPV p16 status
Gold standard initial investigation in all neck masses

right.title: Open Incisional or Excisional Biopsy
points: Incises skin, platysma, and cervical fascial compartments
Spills malignant cells directly into surrounding muscular beds
Creates dense scarring that impedes subsequent neck dissection
Proscribed until all endoscopic evaluations are completed

steps.tx: The workup for an unknown primary incorporates high-resolution cross-sectional contrast imaging and positron emission tomography coupled with formal examination under anesthesia, termed panendoscopy or triple endoscopy. Panendoscopy encompasses direct laryngoscopy, bronchoscopy, and esophagoscopy. Even if mucosal surfaces appear visually normal, surgeons perform **directed diagnostic mucosal biopsies**, specifically bilaterally harvesting palatine tonsils via tonsillectomy, base of tongue mucosectomy, and sampling the nasopharyngeal fossa of Rosenmuller where microscopic occult tumors lurk.
steps.say: Workup of an unknown primary requires PET imaging and examination under anesthesia with directed biopsies of the palatine tonsils, tongue base, and nasopharynx.

nodes.label: FNAC Confirms Squamous Cell Carcinoma (p16 Testing)
Whole-Body FDG PET-CT Cross-Sectional Scan
Examination Under Anesthesia & Triple Endoscopy
Directed Bilateral Tonsillectomy & Tongue Base Mucosectomy
Identification of Occult Primary in Over 70% of Cases

steps.tx: In stark contrast to chronic neoplastic or granulomatous lymphadenopathy, acute cervical cellulitis presents with fulminant airway and septic compromise. The most lethal variant is **Ludwig angina**, an aggressive, rapidly spreading, gangrenous cellulitis involving the submandibular, sublingual, and submental fascial spaces bilaterally. Characteristically non-suppurative and devoid of true initial abscess formation, it produces a tense, woody or brawny induration of the entire submandibular region and floor of mouth.
steps.say: Ludwig angina is a rapidly spreading, gangrenous cellulitis affecting the submandibular, submental, and sublingual spaces bilaterally, causing board-like woody neck swelling.

left.title: Ludwig Angina
points: Bilateral involvement of sublingual and submandibular spaces
Gangrenous cellulitis with woody, brawny, non-fluctuant induration
Elevates and displaces tongue backward into posterior oropharynx
Lethal risk: acute upper airway suffocation within hours

right.title: Acute Peritonsillar Abscess (Quinsy)
points: Unilateral suppurative collection between tonsil capsule and constrictor
Deviates the uvula toward the contralateral unaffected side
Produces severe trismus with hot potato muffled speech
Managed with needle aspiration or intraoral incision and drainage

steps.tx: The etiology in over eighty percent of patients with Ludwig angina is odontogenic infection originating from the mandibular second and third molars. Because the roots of these posterior molars extend beneath the attachment line of the mylohyoid muscle on the internal mandibular surface, a periapical abscess erodes through the thin lingual cortical bone directly into the submandibular space. The microbial flora is polymicrobial, predominantly consisting of oral viridans streptococci, Peptostreptococcus, Fusobacterium, and **Prevotella anaerobes**.
steps.say: Over eighty percent of cases arise from infected second or third lower molars, whose roots penetrate below the mylohyoid ridge, releasing mixed streptococcal and anaerobic flora.

nodes.label: Periapical Abscess in Mandibular 2nd or 3rd Molar
Molar Roots Extend Below Mylohyoid Line
Erosion Through Thin Lingual Mandibular Cortex
Direct Spread into Submandibular & Sublingual Spaces
Rapid Bilateral Cellulitis with Airway Displacement

steps.tx: A patient with Ludwig angina presents with high fever, severe submandibular pain, drooling, inability to swallow secretions, trismus, and a muffled hot-potato voice. As edema expands, the sublingual space swells, pushing the tongue superiorly and backward against the posterior pharyngeal wall, producing catastrophic **upper airway obstruction**. Stridor, tachypnea, cyanosis, and the tripod position indicate impending complete asphyxiation, making immediate definitive airway securing the absolute paramount resuscitation priority.
steps.say: Sublingual edema forces the tongue backward against the pharynx, threatening imminent asphyxiation. Patients exhibit drooling, stridor, and a muffled voice, demanding immediate airway control.

rows: Massive Tongue Protrusion
Sublingual compartment edema lifting floor of mouth
Mandates immediate preparation for emergent surgical airway
Drooling & Odynophagia

Suction secretions, place patient in high Fowler or forward-leaning posture
Inspiratory Stridor

Absolute red flag: endotracheal intubation or awake fiberoptic scope
Woody Neck Induration

steps.tx: Management of Ludwig angina is governed by three cardinal pillars: securing the airway, administering high-dose intravenous antibiotics, and performing aggressive surgical decompression. Endotracheal intubation is fraught with peril due to distorted landmarks, making **awake fiberoptic intubation** or surgical tracheostomy the safest approaches. Surgical decompression employs a wide, curved collar incision across the upper neck, dividing the platysma and mylohyoid muscles to release compartment pressure, extract the offending tooth, and place through-and-through drains.
steps.say: Management requires awake fiberoptic intubation or tracheostomy, high-dose intravenous antibiotics, and wide surgical decompression dividing the mylohyoid muscle to release pressure.

nodes.label: Awake Fiberoptic Intubation or Surgical Tracheostomy
High-Dose IV Ceftriaxone, Metronidazole & Vancomycin

Divide Mylohyoid Muscle to Decompress Compartments
Extraction of Offending Molars & Dependent Drain Placement
